title: 0004-bradley-terry-elo-unification
universal_lens: The Bradley-Terry and Élő paradigms are unified by representing the pairwise win-probability matrix as a sigmoid-transformed structured log-odds matrix. The classical Bradley-Terry-Élô model emerges as an antisymmetric, rank-two special case of this general linear algebraic structure.
gsi_mapping: GSI maps the structured log-odds matrix to a Bayesian latent variable model. Team skill factors become posterior distributions updated via gradient ascent on the log-likelihood, with nuclear-norm regularization enforcing low-rank priors over the competitive state space.
gse_mapping: GSE treats the online learning scheme as a discrete-time state-transition operator. Match outcomes trigger localized updates to team factor vectors, while covariates (e.g., home advantage) act as situational bias fields modifying the underlying transition probabilities.

primitives.breakdown_regime: Diverges or oscillates if the K-factor is too large relative to the variance of the score differences; sensitive to the ordering of incoming match data.

layer2.telemetry: Convergence speed and stability of the validation log-likelihood during hyperparameter tuning.

reasoning_traces.think:
The unification of Bradley-Terry and Élô rests on recognizing both as maximum likelihood estimators for a logistic model of paired comparisons. By defining the log-odds matrix L such that P = \sigma(L), we abstract the probability generation into a structural constraint on L. The classic Élô system corresponds to an antisymmetric, rank-two L, where L_{ij} = \theta_i - \theta_j. This elegant representation allows systematic extensions: adding a constant term yields home advantage, while introducing additional factor matrices (e.g., L = u v^T - v u^T) creates higher-rank models capturing nuanced team interactions. However, empirical tests on English Premier League data reveal that these higher-rank extensions fail to outperform the simple rank-two model, suggesting that the added expressivity merely fits noise rather than signal. The online learning formulation interprets the Élô update rule as single-sample stochastic gradient ascent on the negative log-likelihood, providing a principled foundation for dynamic rating adjustments. Crucially, the failure of complex models underscores the importance of regularization and parsimony in high-dimensional sports analytics, validating the continued use of the foundational antisymmetric kernel despite its apparent simplicity.

reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: Bradley and Terry (1952) introduced the probabilistic model for paired comparisons, establishing the logistic link function. Élô (1978) adapted this for chess ratings, introducing the dynamic update mechanism and K-factor. Király and Qian (2017) retrospectively unified these by framing Élô as an online MLE procedure for the Bradley-Terry model, embedding both within a broader matrix factorization paradigm that connects sports analytics to collaborative filtering and recommendation systems.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Teams are modeled as rational agents whose latent skill levels determine their probability of winning. The model assumes teams play optimally given their current state, and outcomes reflect the true difference in skill plus random noise. The online update mechanism implicitly models teams as adaptive entities whose skills evolve over time, though the paper notes that temporal dynamics are handled heuristically rather than through a rigorous state-space model.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Higher-rank models must be vetoed if they do not demonstrate statistically significant improvement in out-of-sample log-likelihood over the baseline rank-two model. Furthermore, any extension incorporating external features (e.g., player injuries, weather) must pass strict anti-collinearity checks to ensure the new features do not merely proxy for the existing skill ratings, preventing double-counting of information and ensuring robust generalization.
